opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this one genuinely surprised me. For a long time, my instinct, and I think the whole industry's instinct, was that latency is everything. Every millisecond matters. You look at search, you look at consumer internet products, and the lesson was always that if you make people wait, they leave. So we spent a lot of energy thinking about how to make responses feel instant.

Then we started shipping reasoning models, where the model actually thinks for a while before answering, sometimes seconds, sometimes minutes. I was honestly nervous about it. I thought people would find it frustrating. What we saw was the opposite, at least for the right kinds of problems. If you're asking something hard, a tricky bug, a complicated analysis, a real research question, people are happy to wait if the answer is meaningfully better. They don't want a fast wrong answer. They want the right answer.

I think the mental model shifted from "this is a search box" to "this is a very capable colleague." If you hand a smart coworker a hard problem, you don't expect them to blurt out a response in half a second. You'd actually be a little suspicious if they did. You expect them to go think about it and come back with something good.

So now I think about it as a spectrum. For quick, casual questions, speed still matters a lot, and we want those to feel instant. But for hard problems, the value of more thinking time is enormous, and I suspect we'll see people comfortable with the model working for hours or even days on really important problems. That's a pretty big change from where my intuitions started. The lesson for me was that people care about the quality of the outcome much more than I'd assumed, as long as they trust that the waiting is actually buying them something.

r001.rationale: The response says people are happy to wait on hard problems when the delay produces a meaningfully better answer.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it really surprised me. For most of the history of software, the rule was obvious: faster is better, every hundred milliseconds of latency costs you users. We internalized that completely. When we were building the first ChatGPT, we agonized over how quickly the tokens streamed back, because we assumed people would get bored and leave.

And then we started shipping models that think before they answer, and we braced for complaints. Instead, people were fine. More than fine, actually. If you tell someone the model is going to spend thirty seconds, or five minutes, or in some cases hours working on a genuinely hard problem, and it comes back with a much better answer, they'll happily wait. They'll go do something else. It turns out what people really care about isn't speed, it's whether the thing gets done right.

What that taught me is that we'd been conflating two very different kinds of interaction. One is conversational, where you want it to feel instant, like talking to a person. The other is delegation, where you hand something off and you care about the outcome, not the latency. Nobody is upset that a good colleague takes a day to write a careful memo. We'd been building for the first mode and hadn't fully noticed the second one was emerging.

The honest version is that my instincts were just wrong, or at least incomplete. I had this very strong prior about user patience that came from a world where software couldn't do anything hard, so waiting was pure cost. Once the model can actually solve the problem, waiting becomes an investment, and people reason about it that way. I think the right design now is to let people choose. Sometimes you want the quick answer, sometimes you want it to really grind. And increasingly I think the interesting products will be the ones where you don't wait at all, you just come back later and the work is done.

r001.rationale: The response says people will happily wait—even minutes or hours—when the model returns a much better answer to a genuinely hard problem.

astra-6.text:
I used to think speed was almost always better—that people wanted the answer immediately, and every extra second was a problem. But people are much more willing to wait if the model is doing something genuinely hard and the answer is substantially better.

If you ask a simple question, you want a fast response. But if you give a model a problem that would take you hours, waiting a few minutes for a good answer can be a great trade. That challenged my instinct that latency was something we should always minimize. What matters is how quickly you get to a useful result, and sometimes that means letting the model think longer.

r001.rationale: The candidate says people are more willing to wait when the model tackles a genuinely hard problem and produces a substantially better answer.

And what surprised me is how willing people are to wait if the model can actually solve a hard problem. If it can do something useful that would otherwise take you hours, waiting a few minutes is a pretty good trade. So I’ve had to update my intuition: the goal isn’t always the fastest response. It’s getting a result that’s worth waiting for.

r001.rationale: The response says people are willing to wait minutes when a model can solve a hard problem and provide a useful result.
